Dynamic Nelson-Siegel Model Implementation

Source: R/dns-model.r
fit_ns_model.Rd

Functions to calibrate and fit the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel (DNS) model to yield curve data.

Fits the Nelson-Siegel model to a single yield curve (cross-section) for a specific date.

Usage

fit_ns_model(
  maturities,
  yields,
  initial_lambda = ns_lambda(3.5),
  lambda_constraint = "constrained",
  lower_bounds = c(-0.1, -0.5, -0.5, 0.01),
  upper_bounds = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.5, 2),
  optimizer = "L-BFGS-B",
  method = c("profile", "optim"),
  control = list()
)

Arguments

maturities

Numeric vector. The maturities (in years) for the yield curve points.

yields

Numeric vector. The yield values corresponding to the maturities.

initial_lambda

Numeric. Initial value for the decay parameter lambda, per unit of maturity, and the value used outright when lambda_constraint = "fixed". Maturities here are in years, and the default places the curvature hump at 3.5 years, near the middle of a Treasury curve; it is written as ns_lambda(3.5) so the number states its own meaning. Diebold and Li's 0.0609 is a month-denominated constant: in years it places the hump at 29.4 years, off the end of most curves, where the slope loading is nearly parallel to the level loading and the two factors are not separately identified. See ns_lambda.

lambda_constraint

Character. One of "fixed", "constrained", or "free":

  • "fixed": lambda is fixed at the initial_lambda value.

  • "constrained": lambda is optimized within bounds.

  • "free": lambda is optimized without constraints.

With method = "optim" the search over lambda is weak: L-BFGS-B's numerical gradient is poorly scaled when the betas are around 0.05 and lambda around 0.5, and in practice lambda moves very little from initial_lambda even when unconstrained. method = "profile" searches lambda properly and reaches the same optimum from any starting value, so prefer it when lambda is meant to be estimated rather than supplied.

lower_bounds

Numeric vector of length 4. Lower bounds for parameters (beta1, beta2, beta3, lambda).

upper_bounds

Numeric vector of length 4. Upper bounds for parameters (beta1, beta2, beta3, lambda). The lambda ceiling is 2, which places the curvature hump at 0.9 years; a ceiling of 0.5 bound the fit on roughly a third of real month-end curves, and a clamped lambda is reported through at_bound rather than silently. Raising it further buys in-sample fit at the cost of comparability across dates, since factors estimated at different lambda are not on the same scale.

optimizer

Character. The optimization method to use. Default is "L-BFGS-B". Used by method = "optim" only.

method

Character. How to solve the fit. "profile" (the default) exploits the fact that the curve is linear in the betas once lambda is fixed: the betas are solved by least squares in closed form, and lambda alone is searched over one dimension, by a log-spaced grid and then a refinement between the bracketing points. "optim" searches all four parameters numerically, as in versions before 0.6.0.

Profiling is the default because it is better on every axis measured over 200 curves from the bundled panel: a lower mean fit error from any starting lambda (5.57 bp against 5.74 from the package default, 8.52 from 0.0609 and 5.97 from 1.5), exact independence of the starting value (a spread of 0.000 bp against 2.775), roughly a third of the run time, and no convergence failures. Where the two disagree on lambda by more than 0.05 – 15 of those 200 curves – the profiled fit is the better of the two on all 15. It also needs no beta start values or beta bounds, which removes a class of boundary solution "optim" can return.

"optim" remains available and is unchanged apart from the scaled objective; pass it to reproduce a fit made with an earlier version.

control

List. Passed to optim's control argument by method = "optim"; ignored by method = "profile", which uses optimize. The objective is minimised in squared basis points so that L-BFGS-B's relative convergence test is genuinely relative, which means factr keeps its documented meaning here and rarely needs changing.

Value

A list containing:

  • parameters: Named vector of fitted parameters (beta1, beta2, beta3, lambda)

  • fitted_yields: Vector of fitted yield values, one per retained maturity

  • rmse: Root mean squared error of the fit

  • maturities: The retained maturities (input maturities, minus any dropped for being missing or non-positive)

  • actual_yields: The retained input yields

  • residuals: The fitting residuals (actual - fitted)

  • success: Logical indicating if the optimization converged

  • valid_idx: Logical vector over the input maturities marking which points were retained, so callers can place the fitted values back into a full-width row

  • at_bound: Named logical vector marking parameters that came to rest on one of their bounds

Details

The Nelson-Siegel model expresses the yield curve as: $$y(m) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m}\right) + \beta_3 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m} - e^{-\lambda m}\right)$$ where \(m\) is maturity, \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\), and \(\beta_3\) represent the level, slope, and curvature factors, respectively, and \(\lambda\) controls the decay rate of factor loadings.

With method = "profile" the sum of squared errors is concentrated: for any lambda the optimal betas are the least-squares solution of \(y = X(\lambda)\beta\), so the objective reduces to a function of lambda alone, minimised over [lower_bounds[4], upper_bounds[4]] by optimize. Beta bounds are not consulted, since the linear solve is exact.

The default bounds are written for yields in decimal form. When they are left at their defaults and the data is evidently on another scale (yields in percentage points, say), the beta box is widened to cover the data rather than clamping the level factor: L-BFGS-B reports convergence at a bound, so a clamped fit would otherwise be returned with success = TRUE. Any parameter that does come to rest on a bound is reported in at_bound and raises a warning.

Examples

maturities <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, 30)
yields <- c(0.0050, 0.0052, 0.0055, 0.0065, 0.0078, 0.0105, 0.0128, 0.0152, 0.0215, 0.0225)
fit_ns_model(maturities, yields)
#> Warning: Nelson-Siegel fit rests on a parameter bound (lambda); the factor decomposition is not identified. Widen lower_bounds/upper_bounds or check the yield scale.
#> Nelson-Siegel curve fit
#>   beta1 (level)     -1.23764
#>   beta2 (slope)     1.24188
#>   beta3 (curvature) 1.52159
#>   lambda            0.01000
#>   rmse              2.65 bp over 10 maturities
#>   at bound          lambda (decomposition not identified)

# The profiled fit solves the betas in closed form at each lambda, so it
# needs no start values and cannot return a clamped beta.
fit_ns_model(maturities, yields, method = "profile")
#> Warning: Nelson-Siegel fit rests on a parameter bound (lambda); the factor decomposition is not identified. Widen lower_bounds/upper_bounds or check the yield scale.
#> Nelson-Siegel curve fit
#>   beta1 (level)     -1.23764
#>   beta2 (slope)     1.24188
#>   beta3 (curvature) 1.52159
#>   lambda            0.01000
#>   rmse              2.65 bp over 10 maturities
#>   at bound          lambda (decomposition not identified)

# A real curve from the bundled panel
data(treasury_yields)
latest <- treasury_yields[nrow(treasury_yields), ]
fit_ns_model(as.numeric(setdiff(names(treasury_yields), "Date")),
             as.numeric(latest[-1]), method = "profile")
#> Nelson-Siegel curve fit
#>   beta1 (level)     0.04927
#>   beta2 (slope)     -0.00515
#>   beta3 (curvature) -0.01551
#>   lambda            0.66877
#>   rmse              4.43 bp over 11 maturities
